catalog_quote: There are no diphthongs and when two vowels are used together each has its full value; 'ai is a word of two separated elements and haeo a word of three. Two consonants can never be used together. Almost all syllables are therefore open. However, in quick speech, where the final and the penultimate vowel are the same and the latter is accentuated, the final vowel is completely lost—laŋisi frequently becomes laŋis. Accentuation generally falls on the penultimate syllable. If the word has only two syllables this means that it is the first which is stressed. So general is this rule that it is only necessary to indicate accentuation in the exceptions. This is done in the following way— awa'ku (stress on ku). new_statements.quote: Accentuation generally falls on the penultimate syllable. If the word has only two syllables this means that it is the first which is stressed. So general is this rule that it is only necessary to indicate accentuation in the exceptions. This is done in the following way—awa'ku (stress on ku). If two words are combined to form a compound each will retain its original accentuation. The word maka has the normal stress; when it is combined with si, the resulting compound is 'maka-'si. Proper names must be mentioned separately. The general rule of penultimate syllable stress still holds provided the proper noun has more than two syllables. If it has only two syllables, then it is always the last which is stressed, e.g. ma'o, pe'i, ho'u, etc.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is regular on the penultimate syllable (hence initial in disyllables); it is predictable enough that Hogbin marks accent only on exceptions. Each member of a compound keeps its own penultimate stress. Disyllabic proper names are the systematic exception, taking final stress; longer proper names follow the penult rule. Stress is not used morphologically ('change of stress [is] never used', p.826). Salmond 1974:226 (seen in Google Books snippets only) agrees and adds detail: stress on the penultimate vowel before each juncture and on every alternate preceding vowel, realized as greater volume, raised pitch and slight lengthening; monovocalic (grammatical) formatives are inherently unstressed; she notes the rule 'is not wholly accurate'. Lanyon-Orgill 1944:8 (snippet): 'Accent is always on the penultimate.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Hogbin says nothing about secondary stress. Salmond 1974:226 (snippet view only): stress falls on the penultimate vowel preceding a juncture 'and each alternate preceding vowel', i.e. alternating rhythmic stress leftward from the penult.
new_statements.exceptions: Hogbin: a few lexical exceptions marked with a stroke before the stressed syllable (e.g. awa'ku, stress on ku); disyllabic proper names always have final stress (ma'o, pe'i, ho'u); in quick speech a word-final vowel identical to the stressed penult vowel is dropped (langisi > langis), leaving surface-final stress. Salmond: formatives with a single vowel cannot take penult stress and are inherently unstressed; 'this stress prediction rule is not wholly accurate, but no more accurate generalization has been found'.
new_statements.domain_note: Hogbin's rule is stated for the word, counted in syllables (every vowel is syllabic: 'there are no diphthongs.. 'ai is a word of two separated elements and haeo a word of three'; vowel length exists but he does not relate it to stress). Compounds: each member is its own stress domain. Salmond's domain is the formative/word before a juncture, counted in vowels.
new_statements.identity_note: Hogbin 1930 describes the language of the whole Ongtong Java atoll ('Ongtong Javanese'), noting the two tribes Pelau (north) and Luaniua (south) speak identically 'in all but a few minor points'; this is glottocode onto1237 (Luangiua, iso ojv). Salmond 1974 ('LUA') and Lanyon-Orgill 1944 ('Leuangiua') describe the same language.

sources.locator: Part I 'Phonetic System', p. 826 (pdf page 863 of the DLI full-volume scan; page 4 of the saved extract)
sources.note: p.826: 'Accentuation generally falls on the penultimate syllable'; disyllables stress the first; exceptions marked with a pre-syllable stroke (awa'ku); compounds keep the stress of each member ('maka-'si); disyllabic proper names are stressed on the final (ma'o, pe'i, ho'u), longer proper names follow the penult rule; in quick speech a final vowel identical to the accented penult vowel is lost (langisi > langis); 'change of stress' is never used morphologically (p.826).
